li.a: ABC News: Jail term completes Einfeld's disgrace
Canberra Times: Former judge Einfeld gets at least two years jail ... all for lying about a $77 traffic fine
ABC Radio National Law Report: The fall of Marcus Einfeld
Green Left: Jailed over a $77 speeding ticket
World Socialist Web Site: The political issues behind the jailing of former Federal Court judge Marcus Einfeld
The Australian, 23 March 2009 (reproduced): Einfeld airs his regrets on TV program
Bendigo Advertiser: Jailed judge plans to seek redemption in charity work
SBS News: Disgraced judge to return to public work

content.p: Marcus Einfeld spent decades as one of Australia's best-known human rights lawyers and judges. He was a justice of the Federal Court, the founding president of the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission, and a man once voted one of the country's "national living treasures". In 2009 he was led from a Sydney courtroom to begin a prison term because of a speeding ticket worth $77.

The ticket was never the crime. The crime was what he did after it. In 2006 he told a court on oath, and then police in a signed statement, that someone else had been driving his car. The person he named had been dead for almost three years. He later pleaded guilty to perjury and to perverting the course of justice, and on 20 March 2009 the Supreme Court of New South Wales passed a three-year jail term on him, with two years before he could seek parole.
content.h2: A lunch, a camera and a form
content.p: Richard Ackland, a Sydney legal journalist who covered the saga for the Sydney Morning Herald and the legal publication Justinian, told ABC radio what happened on 8 January 2006. Einfeld had taken a former girlfriend, Vivian Schenker, to lunch at a smart restaurant near Freshwater. His partner, his mother and his stepdaughter were at the theatre. On the drive home in his silver Lexus, a speed camera photographed the car in Mosman at about 60 kilometres an hour in a 50 zone.

The penalty was small. Most pages put the fine at $77; the World Socialist Web Site and Ackland said $75. Green Left reported that it carried three demerit points. At sentencing, Justice James noted that Einfeld had only four points left on his licence, which meant that a conviction would have left him with one. That, the prosecution argued, was why he lied: to avoid demerit points.

According to Ackland, Einfeld first signed the back of the penalty notice and declared that he had not been driving. That declaration seemed to go missing in the system, and the state's penalty processing bureau instead sent him a notice to attend court. Ackland said Einfeld could have corrected the record at that point. Instead he wrote a long letter to the court's chief presiding officer insisting he had not been the driver and asking to give evidence.

On 7 August 2006, the WSWS reported, Einfeld told a Local Court magistrate that a friend, Professor Teresa Brennan, who lived in the United States, had been driving. The magistrate accepted the statement and cancelled the fine, the same source said. (The Bendigo Advertiser dates his contest of the ticket to August 2007; the Canberra Times and the WSWS say August 2006.)

A court reporter from the Daily Telegraph, Viva Goldner, was in the room. Ackland said she and an editor went online to find a photograph of Brennan to illustrate the story. They could not find one. They found instead that Brennan, an Australian-born professor at a Florida university, had died in February 2003, almost three years before the speeding offence. ABC News said Einfeld told a court she had died in a hit-and-run accident; the Bendigo Advertiser described her death as a car accident in the United States.

Goldner telephoned Einfeld at home and put the inconsistency to him. His answer, as Ackland told it, was that there were two Teresa Brennans: this was a different one, also an Australian professor living in the United States, who had also died in a car accident but at a later date. The Bendigo Advertiser reported that Einfeld told a journalist it was a different Teresa Brennan and produced a document describing this second, fictitious woman. Ackland called the excuse "completely infantile".

The newspaper story set off a police investigation. By then, Ackland said, Einfeld had a new problem: the perjury itself. He signed a lengthy statement for police on 23 August 2006, which Ackland described as a second plan. In it, Ackland said, Einfeld now claimed he had not been in Foster, as he had told the court, but had lunched with Schenker. He said he had been driving his mother's car, and that he had lent the Lexus to a second Professor Brennan whose first name he could not pin down. That statement became the basis for the second charge, perverting the course of justice.

Einfeld also tried to rely on another woman. Schenker, a former journalist and media adviser to the former Labor leader Mark Latham, was named in ABC's account as the person Einfeld later said he had been with in a different car. ABC News reported that CCTV footage showed that car sitting in a garage all day. The WSWS said the police inquiry traced his movements on 8 January through mobile phone and credit card use.

A Sydney woman, Angela Liati, came forward and said she had driven with "Theresa Brennan" on the date on the ticket. In February 2009 she was found guilty in a separate hearing of making a false police statement by saying she had been the other woman in Einfeld's car. ABC News said she was due to be sentenced in May and had appealed the verdict. Another newspaper account, written in 2011, said she was convicted of attempting to pervert the course of justice and given community service.

Einfeld had said he would fight the charges. ABC News reported that he changed course, to general surprise, when he pleaded guilty a week before the trial was due to start in October 2008. Five other charges had been dropped weeks earlier. The WSWS said his plea meant he avoided prosecution over other speeding infringements, which it said he had also dodged over the years by claiming overseas friends had been driving his car.

At the sentencing hearing, his barrister, Ian Barker QC, asked for a sentence that did not involve jail. Barker described Einfeld as a "beacon of light, a living treasure and a man of honour", and the defence pointed to his prostate cancer and depression. His psychiatrist, Dr Jonathon Phillips, told the court Einfeld had received treatment for depression in 1996 and again in 2006, and had also been diagnosed with prostate cancer. An Aboriginal elder, Madeline McGrady, praised his work with Indigenous communities during his time as human rights commissioner. The Crown prosecutor, Wayne Roser SC, argued for full-time custody and said the counts were in "the worst case category".

Justice Bruce James took all of that into account, including the damage to Einfeld's reputation and his medical condition, but still imposed three years. He called the offending "planned criminal activity" and "deliberate, premeditated perjury", and said it struck "at the heart of the administration of justice". Ackland said the judge described it as "conscious, deliberate, step-by-step criminality", not a quick lie told under surprise questioning, and that reading out the sentencing remarks alone took more than two hours. The judge also said that "any lawyer and especially a lawyer who has been a barrister and a judge" who commits such an offence is sentenced on the basis that he knew its gravity. According to Green Left, the judge ruled out a suspended sentence and periodic detention as insufficient. The Australian noted that Einfeld had not directly apologised in court, and that the judge had pointed this out.

Outside court, Detective Superintendent Colin Dyson, who headed the Fraud Squad, said: "For the sake of a small monetary penalty, people's lives can be absolutely ruined." He said the investigation had not been treated as the pursuit of a speeding fine, but as a case about what followed it, and that it had been given the same priority as any other. The Canberra Times quoted him as saying that only Einfeld knew why he had done it.

The scene in the courtroom was widely reported. Supporters filled the room, some sitting on the floor, and several hugged Einfeld at the dock. ABC News said he stumbled and grabbed the rail as the sentence was read. Einfeld told a supporter, "the bag is packed".

Three days after the sentence, Einfeld appeared on the ABC program Four Corners. "I lied. I can't say it any simpler than that," he said. "I told a lie which was a disgraceful thing to do and for which I've been paying ever since." He said using Brennan's name, a friend, was "probably more shameful than the driving". He also denied that his untruths were part of a longstanding pattern, telling the program he had simply made a mistake. The reporter, Sarah Ferguson, thought his aim in taking part was to have his career weighed alongside his crimes.

Not everyone thought the sentence fair. Green Left reported that an email circulated in early March 2009 pleaded to keep him out of prison and praised the respect he commanded in the profession. The World Socialist Web Site called the term "grossly disproportionate" and argued that the media and police pursuit of him may have been politically motivated, pointing to Einfeld's clashes with the Howard government. That is the view of a political website, and it offered no court finding to support it. In 2011 Einfeld himself said the sentence was "unbalanced" and that everyone knew it was "more political than anything else".

Einfeld was held first at Long Bay and then at Silverwater. The Bendigo Advertiser reported that he gave up his Order of Australia and his commission as Queen's Counsel and stepped down from the New South Wales Bar Association while inside; SBS said the Queen's Counsel title had been stripped from him in 2008. The Canberra Times said he lost his place on the legal roll, his Queen's Counsel status and his Order of Australia.

He was released on Saturday 19 March 2011, after serving two years, and was to report to a parole officer for 12 months. Aged 72, he said he planned to return to public work, "subject to recovering my health", with a focus on prison reform and on mental health among prisoners. He called the period "the worst period of my life".

In an interview that September, he said jail had made him lose his faith and that being parted from his children was the hardest part. He described his time in the prison as being in "the Hilton Hotel wing". He said he had a private room and could use a kitchen. His mother, Billie, died aged 99 soon after his release. He called the crime a "silly snap moment" and said he planned a foundation for mental health in prisons. He added that these days he drives "very slowly".
